Malfatti Zoom

GeometryCirclesTriangles
Game: Three circles sit inside a triangle, each touching two sides and the other two circles.
How to play: Drag the three corner dots to change the triangle, tick what you want to see, and press a Zoom button to look closer.
Look for the math

Malfatti asked for three circles in a triangle, each touching the other two and two sides. Steiner found a way to build them, and Hart proved it works no matter what shape the triangle has. The zoom exists so you can check the faraway intersection points when a triangle gets skewed.

Steiner's construction, with subscripts

Write the corners as A₁ A₂ A₃ and let I be the incenter. For each corner A_i there is a small incircle c_i in the triangle formed by I and the other two corners. The angle bisectors through I are common internal tangents of pairs of these small circles. Take the other internal tangent of each pair: the three lines meet at L and cut the sides at D₁, D₂, D₃.

Why the three circles fit

Each quadrilateral A_i D_j L D_k has an incircle, and those three incircles are the Malfatti circles. Equal tangent segments from a point to one circle are the key: they make the common tangent of two final circles pass through the same D_i that the construction drew. Testing thousands of triangles here confirms it: the final circles touch one another and the two sides at their own corner, to within about a millionth of a board unit. The three small incircles touch their two bisectors, and the tangents really do concur at L.

Every configuration, and a pixel quirk

Hart's proof has to cope with the line through D_i and L meeting the perimeter on different sides in different triangles. When E₁ and E₃ fall on the same side, the circle inscribed in the triangle bounded by L E₁, L E₃ and that side touches it at D₂; the page says only that this "appears", and here it holds to within a pixel. The applet chooses the second tangent by asking whether it is more than one pixel from I. On thin triangles both tangents can be closer than that, so it falls back to the bisector and the displayed circles no longer touch exactly: in a 600-triangle sweep the worst miss was under half a unit. This port keeps that quirk and reports it in the status line; zooming does not change the geometry, only the view.

Not the marble problem

The original question asked for marble columns of the greatest total volume, which becomes packing three circles of the largest total area in a triangle. Malfatti assumed the circles touch each other and two sides, but they are not the largest packing: in an equilateral triangle the incircle plus two corner circles wins. Hart's proof is about the touching construction, not about maximizing area; the intermediate value theorem is what makes the continuous version of his argument rigorous.

Try the four checkboxes one at a time, then drag a corner until the status says the circles miss: that is the applet's one-pixel test failing.
